tones.name: Neutral
tones.description: General writing for no particular audience.

tones.name: Slack
tones.description: Workplace chat with colleagues. Short messages, fragments, lowercase sentence starts, emoji and common chat abbreviations (pls, thx, btw, imo, afaik, lmk) are normal. It should read like a chat message, not an email.

tones.name: GitHub
tones.description: Comments on issues, pull requests and discussions. Concise, technical, direct but polite. Markdown, code identifiers and developer shorthand (PR, LGTM, WIP, IMO, nit:, repro) are normal; other chat abbreviations are not.

tones.name: Formal email
tones.description: Professional email to a client, a manager or someone the writer doesn't know well. Full sentences, no chat abbreviations, contractions only sparingly. In German, use Sie.

tones.name: Friends
tones.description: Personal messages to friends. Anything natural in speech is fine: slang, abbreviations, missing punctuation. In German, use du.

languages.summary: Word order after weil and dass is now consistently right; that pattern is mastered. The dative after 'mit' is improving and was right in your recent texts. 'Eine Entscheidung treffen' still slips back to 'machen' now and then.
languages.tip: 'Mit' always takes the dative: mit dem Kunden, mit der Kollegin, mit den Kollegen.

languages.summary: Finished times like 'yesterday' and 'last week' now come with the past simple; that one is mastered. 'Yet' with the present perfect is the next thing to watch.
languages.tip: 'Yet' pairs with the present perfect: 'He hasn't answered yet.'
